reclassified.finding: Reading the module whole shows it is not an admission gate but a tier-seating pass. For every plugin the managed settings enable it decides whether that plugin's hooks load in the organization's tier or the user's, and it withholds the organization's tier - with a warning naming which condition failed - when the plugin does not load in place from a local folder its marketplace is registered from, when the source it is registered from is named only by a managed settings source the session does not vouch for (remote managed settings the server has not confirmed this session, or a document the user account can write), and when no managed source names that source at all. The generalisable half is stated outright: a managed settings source on this machine was not read whole (a load error, or a plugin key it could not apply), so what it says of plugins is not known.
reclassified.localCheck: The not-read-whole half is already enforced here more strongly: src/config.ts:938-944 reads the one managed settings file as required and rejects any key outside allowShell, permissions, features and mcpClient, and readSettingsLayer (src/config.ts:414) throws on a missing required file, an oversize file, invalid JSON and a non-object, so a managed source that cannot be read whole aborts configuration instead of being treated as having spoken. The seating half has nothing to land on: no plugin tier, no marketplace registration, no enabledPlugins list and no remote managed settings source exist here, and src/plugins.ts plugins are inert local directory snapshots discovered from a store index by digest with pluginConfigSchema a single enabled switch plus size limits, so nothing carries an organization identity to seat or withhold. The principle underneath - a source the governed party can write must not count as the governing party's policy - is already enforced where it applies: a project layer cannot approve its own MCP servers (src/config.ts:962-968, W12), and the managed file is named by the caller rather than discovered.
reclassified.whyNotPorted: Porting the seating rule would mean building a plugin tier, a marketplace registration model and a remote managed settings source first. That is new product scope rather than a rule landing on a surface this runtime already owns, so it is recorded as a rule without a local surface rather than as a pending port.

reclassified.wasCandidate: external instruction-file imports behind a forward-scoped consent dialog
reclassified.finding: The module is the dialog, not the rule. It renders a warning-titled question - "Allow external CLAUDE.md file imports?" with the body "This project's CLAUDE.md or .claude/rules imports files outside the current working directory. Never allow this for third-party repositories." - lists the external imports it found, states that a yes covers "any this project adds later", records the answer and latches a refusal so the question is not asked again in the same scope. Everything it gates is a surface this runtime does not have: an instruction import that leaves the working directory is refused, so there is nothing to ask about.
reclassified.localCheck: Both places that would decide it refuse instead of asking. At configuration time the nested-import visitor throws for any import that realpaths outside the root, with the reserved-tree and depth refusals beside it (src/config.ts:1173; W10 ported the link-chain half of the same visitor and recorded this consent as not ported). At tool time an out-of-workspace path is refused outright rather than asked about: "path escapes the workspace (absolute paths are not allowed)" (src/tools.ts:136), with the symlink and dangling-symlink spellings at :140, :168 and :173. Nothing in src/ prompts for out-of-workspace file access. The corpus note recorded the containment rule's site as src/config.ts:1136 when the band was read; the throw is at :1173 and the earlier number addresses the installed-plugin index recheck, so the citation is corrected here.
reclassified.whyNotPorted: The reusable half of this candidate is not the dialog but its shape - a capability a checkout asks for, granted only by a person, where one yes stands for what that checkout adds later - and that shape already landed here on the surface this runtime has, as W12's project-declared MCP server approval, which keys the answer to the declaration digest and the workspace real path, refuses to let a checkout answer for itself (src/config.ts:962-968) and takes the one standing switch from the user layer. Porting this module's consent would instead add an interactive, forward-scoped grant whose only effect is to relax the confinement that refuses the import: new product scope in the direction of less confinement, not a rule landing on a surface this runtime owns.
reclassified.ledgerEffect: none; the module stays uncited because nothing in the product cites it
